summary: Defines the SIP Pending Additions event package. SIP relays use it to tell user agents about the consent-related status of entries that are to be added to a resource list. It is a standards-track document that works with the SIP consent framework.

eli5.summary: When you invite people to a group, some have not yet said yes. This lets the relay tell you who is still waiting for permission to join.

questions: consent status of resource list entries

subtitle: How a SIP relay tells you which people you are adding to a list have actually agreed to hear from it.

tldr.problem: A user who adds recipients to a relay's translation logic needs to know which of them have given the relay permission to send them SIP requests.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5362 defines the consent-pending-additions SIP event package. A user agent subscribes, and the relay sends NOTIFY requests carrying a resource list in which each entry has a consent-status of pending, waiting, error, denied or granted.
tldr.outcome: Subscribers get either the full list each time or, optionally, small XML patch updates. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is not obsoleted or updated by any other RFC.

facts.label: Notification rate
facts.value: No faster than once every 5 seconds (RECOMMENDED)

today: RFC 5362 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2008. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and it works with the consent framework in RFC 5360.

sections.title: Why Consent Status Needs Reporting
sections.content:
The framework for consent-based communications in SIP, RFC 5360, says that a user changing the translation logic at a relay (for example by adding a new recipient) must be told the consent-related status of the recipients. In other words, the user needs to know which recipients have given the relay permission to send them SIP requests.

A relay here means any SIP server, whether a proxy, a B2BUA or a hybrid, that receives a request, translates its Request-URI into one or more next-hop URIs and delivers the request to them. RFC 5362 defines a SIP event package that lets user agents subscribe to the consent state of resources being added to a resource list that defines such a translation.
sections.eli5: Imagine you add friends to a group chat, but each friend has to say yes first. This tells you who has said yes and who has not.

sections.title: How the Pieces Fit Together
sections.content:
A user agent subscribes to a relay using the Pending Additions event package. NOTIFY requests in this package carry an XML document in one of two formats: application/resource-lists+xml (from RFC 4826) or application/resource-lists-diff+xml, which is based on XML patch operations from RFC 5261.

A document in the first format gives the whole list of resources being added, with the consent-related status of each. A document in the second format gives only the changes since the last notification sent to that user agent.
sections.eli5: You can ask the relay for the whole guest list every time, or just for a note saying what changed since last time.

sections.title: The consent-status Element
sections.content:
The RFC defines a <consent-status> element in the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:consent-status. Documents MUST be well-formed and SHOULD be valid, MUST be based on XML 1.0 and MUST be encoded in UTF-8. The element holds one of five string values:

  • pending: the relay has received a request to add the resource and will ask for permission.
  • waiting: the relay has asked for permission but has had no answer yet.
  • error: the relay asked and got an error response, so the permission document could not be delivered to the resource.
  • denied: the resource has refused permission.
  • granted: the resource has given permission.
sections.eli5: Each person on the list has a sticker: not asked yet, asked and waiting, could not reach, said no, or said yes.

sections.title: The Event Package Definition
sections.content:
The package name is consent-pending-additions, carried in the Event and Allow-Events header fields as defined by RFC 3265. It defines no event package parameters. Support for the core package definition is REQUIRED; support for partial notifications is optional, but a subscriber that signals it makes Section 6 mandatory.

A SUBSCRIBE MAY carry a body to filter the subscription, but filter documents are not specified in this RFC. Without a body, the default policy applies: notifications are generated every time any resource in the list changes state. The default subscription expiration is one hour (3600 seconds).

NOTIFY bodies are resource list documents. All subscribers and notifiers MUST support application/resource-lists+xml and SHOULD support application/resource-lists-diff+xml. If a SUBSCRIBE has no Accept header field, the default is application/resource-lists+xml; if it has one, it MUST include that type.
sections.eli5: You sign up for updates with a special name, and unless you say otherwise your sign-up lasts for an hour.

sections.title: Notifier and Subscriber Behavior
sections.content:
A notifier SHOULD include the <consent-status> element, positioned as an instance of the <any> element within the <entry> element. Notifications SHOULD be sent whenever the consent state of a resource changes. Once a resource moves to error, denied or granted and a NOTIFY has been sent, it is removed from further notifications.

With full-state documents the subscriber SHOULD update its local information from the document and does not need to aggregate anything. Because the state of a resource list normally sits in one repository, a subscriber MUST NOT create multiple dialogs from one subscription request, so forking is not supported. The server is RECOMMENDED not to notify a single subscriber more often than once every 5 seconds. State agents have no role in this package.
sections.eli5: The relay sends a new update whenever someone's answer changes, but not more than once every few seconds, and it stops mentioning people whose answer is final.

sections.title: Partial Notifications
sections.content:
Sending the whole list for every small change is wasteful in bandwidth-constrained environments. A subscriber signals support for partial notifications by listing application/resource-lists-diff+xml in the Accept header field of its SUBSCRIBE. The server then MAY use that format instead of the full one.

The first notification MUST carry full state. For a partial notification the server sets the Content-Type to application/resource-lists-diff+xml and SHOULD include only what changed, using <add>, <remove> and <replace> elements. It MUST NOT send another partial NOTIFY until it has a final response to the previous one or that request has timed out. On a refresh or termination SUBSCRIBE it SHOULD send the full document.

The subscriber stores the first full document as its local copy, replaces it when another full document arrives and applies patches when a diff arrives. If patch processing fails, the subscriber SHOULD renew the subscription, and can fall back by leaving the diff format out of the new SUBSCRIBE.
sections.eli5: Instead of re-sending the whole guest list, the relay can just say "Bill changed to yes". If you get confused, you can ask for the whole list again.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The state of resources being added can reveal sensitive information, so all subscriptions SHOULD be authenticated and then authorized, with the authorization policy left to the administrator. The RFC RECOMMENDS strong authentication and confidentiality for subscriptions, and strong integrity protection because attackers may try to modify notifications.

Relays are RECOMMENDED to authenticate subscribers with normal SIP mechanisms such as Digest. Further security discussion is in RFC 5360.
sections.eli5: Who said yes or no is private, so the relay should check who you are before telling you.
